abstract:
Striae gravidarum (SG) is a common skin condition characterized by disrupted dermal extracellular matrix (ECM) homeostasis. Despite its high prevalence, the underlying cellular and molecular pathogenesis remains poorly understood, particularly regarding fibroblast heterogeneity and metabolic dysregulation.
To delineate the cellular landscape and molecular mechanisms of SG at single-cell resolution, with a focus on fibroblast subpopulation dynamics, intercellular communication and metabolic reprogramming.
We performed integrated single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNAseq) and single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNAseq) on dermal specimens from human SG lesions and matched healthy skin. Functional validation was conducted using quantitative polymerase chain reaction, histological staining (haematoxylin and eosin, Elastica van Gieson, picrosirius red), immunofluorescence and Mendelian randomization analysis.
SG skin exhibited significant cellular reorganization, with fibroblasts showing the most profound transcriptional changes. Intercellular communication analysis identified a dysregulated sender-receiver axis between the inflammatory, metabolically active sC7 subset and the reparative sC5 subset. Pseudotime analysis indicated blocked differentiation from sC7 to sC5. The sC7 subset underwent specific fatty acid metabolic reprogramming, marked by the upregulation of key enzymes, including ACSBG1. Triacsin C treatment in primary podoplanin (PDPN)+ reticular fibroblasts suppressed ECM gene expression and attenuated profibrotic markers; notably, it also downregulated representative sC7-associated genes while upregulating sC5-associated genes, suggesting partial restoration of a reparative transcriptional programme. Furthermore, local Acsbg1 silencing in dorsal skin alleviated SG-like dermal remodelling in the mouse model, with improved dermal architecture, collagen organization and elastic fibre integrity.
Targeting ACSBG1-mediated fatty acid metabolic reprogramming in profibrotic fibroblast subsets restores a reparative transcriptional programme and ameliorates dermal ECM disruption in SG. These findings identify ACSBG1 as a potential therapeutic target for SG.

Language="eng"><AbstractText>Striae gravidarum (pronounced stry-ee grah-vid-air-um) is a common skin condition. It is also known as pregnancy ‘stretch marks’. It affects a large number of pregnant women worldwide. The condition involves thinning of the skin and disruption of supportive tissue. Women with this condition have visible lines on their skin. Although not harmful, these lines can cause psychological distress. The exact causes of the stretch marks are not well understood. Our study was done in China. We wanted to determine how the stretch marks are formed. To do this, we looked at skin samples from women with stretch marks. The samples were compared with healthy skin without stretch marks using advanced lab techniques. Technology called single-cell RNA sequencing allows us to see the gene activity in individual cells. In particular, we examined fibroblasts. These are cells that produce skin structure components. We found that there is major imbalance in different subtypes of fibroblasts in stretch marks. Cells that promote inflammation and scarring expand. Cells responsible for repair and maintenance shrink. The processing of fats by a particular subset of fibroblasts changes. This process is driven by an enzyme called ACSBG1. If we blocked ACSBG1, there was a reduction in the production of skin-damaging proteins. We also showed that consuming some dietary fatty acids can increase the risk of stretch marks. Our conclusions are that stretch marks are not just a cosmetic issue. They involve metabolic dysregulation and inflammation. These findings present new possibilities for prevention or treatment. This could be beneficial to pregnant women at risk of stretch marks.</AbstractText><CopyrightInformation>© The Author(s) 2026.
